items.title: Many Cubans voted for Trump - now they're turning on Republican immigration policies
items.summary: President Trump's fellow Republicans might feel the brunt of frustration among Cubans at the ballot box, writes the BBC's Will Grant.
items.content:
Since the Trump administration launched its crackdown on undocumented immigrants two years ago, the waiting room of Cuban-born immigration lawyer, Ismael Labrador, in Miami is never empty. His appointment book is packed with relatives of detained immigrants trying to secure their release before they're deported back to their countries of origin.

"We have relatives living in fear right now, we've had relatives who have been deported back to Cuba, unfortunately," he explains.

Cubans have traditionally enjoyed favoured immigration status in the United States under provisions enshrined in 1960s-era legislation called the Cuban Adjustment Act. But widespread arrests across Florida by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents have left the Cuban American community more vulnerable in the US than they'd ever imagined, says Labrador.

"The way I put it is that if you don't have a Green Card in the United States, you may be a target."

Countless mobile phone videos have recorded such arrests in places previously considered off-limits: parents detained outside schoolyards, at bus stops, youth sporting events and even inside courthouses at pre-arranged immigration hearings.

Few have had the impact of the footage of 39-year-old Ecuadorean immigrant, Grace Calero, and her 19-year-old daughter, Giulianna Carriel, being arrested in a hospital ward.

Two months ago, the pair were driving to work in Kissimmee, central Florida when they were hit by another car and taken to hospital in an ambulance. While they were being treated for their injuries, ICE agents burst in and arrested them. They were deported back to Ecuador within days.

Labrador's cousin has also been caught up in the dragnet of ICE detentions. Despite his best efforts, the immigration lawyer was unable to prevent his own relative from being deported back to Cuba.

"It's hard when you're fighting against a lot of resources," he laments.

The Trump administration has repeatedly said the president was elected on a promise to deliver mass deportations and is delivering on that. "He stopped the invasion of our country and as a result of his policies more than 3 million illegal aliens have left the US," a White House spokeswoman told the BBC last week.

ICE, meanwhile, has said it is targeting anyone who has broken American immigration law and is in the country illegally.

IN DEPTH: The real reasons there are so few young US politicians

NEWSLETTER: Sign up for Anthony Zurcher's analysis in your inbox

Labrador was among the 68% of Cuban Americans in Florida who voted for Donald Trump two years ago, a decision he roundly regrets today.

Few could accuse Trump of hiding his plans on immigration. On the campaign trail in 2024, he touted his policy of mass deportations of undocumented migrants.

"On Day One, I will launch the largest deportation programme in American history", he said repeatedly at rallies, including in Florida.

Labrador – and many thousands of disillusioned Latino voters like him – thought the administration would only deport people with criminal records.

"I think we got blindsided by the administration," he argues.

"Personally, I voted for Trump because I wanted to get criminals out of the country," he says, alleging that "communists came in from Cuba under Biden."

"We wanted to have a safe America. We never thought that he was going to go after everybody."

Labrador is far from the only Cuban American in Florida to experience buyer's remorse over President Trump.

Congresswoman Maria Elvira Salazar, who represents Florida's 27th Congressional district, recently released a video filmed outside the White House in which she distanced herself from his deportation policy saying it had gone "too far".

"The same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today," she said, addressing President Trump.

Salazar is locked in a tight race against another Cuban American, the Democratic Party's candidate, Eliott Rodríguez. Her close association with Trump on immigration could potentially cost Salazar her congressional seat.

Florida remains a Trump stronghold. At a recent gathering of Cuban American entrepreneurs in Miami, the atmosphere remained staunchly pro-Trump. "Miami loves Trump, Cuban Americans love Trump," says real estate businessman, Juan Omar Sixto, motioning at the other guests behind him.

"They agree with Trump that anyone who crossed the border illegally should be out," he says, despite acknowledging he illegally entered the US himself six decades earlier.

A poll released on Thursday , external by Florida International University found that not all South Florida Cubans agree - 76% said they disapprove of the Trump administration's deportations of Cubans with no criminal record. But their support for the Republican Party remains steadfast, with 68% saying they plan to vote Republican in November.

In other parts of the country, support amongst Latinos is declining.

In the last election, Trump beat Kamala Harris by 56.1% to 43% - the biggest margin of victory for a candidate in the state since 1988 - in part because of the support of Latino communities. But a recent NBC News/Telemundo poll of 8,000 registered Latino voters showed nearly 60% favour seeing Congress come under Democratic Party control to just 35% wanting a Republican victory.

The high cost of living is a big factor for people's discontent, as residents feel supermarket and petrol prices are impossibly high for working families.

But for many Hispanics, it's also partly because of stories like Heydi Sanchez's.

Sanchez left Cuba in 2019 as the island spiralled into economic collapse and illegally crossed the border from Mexico into the US. After nine months in a detention centre, she was released under an i-220B Order of Supervision which grants the right to remain in the US but carries the constant threat of deportation.

Sanchez settled in Tampa where she worked with autistic children and the elderly. After a complex and expensive fertility struggle, she and her husband had a baby girl called Kailyn.

Most i-220B holders try to normalise their immigration status via 'humanitarian parole' and must check in with ICE agents at regular scheduled appointments. Last year, President Trump revoked temporary humanitarian parole to about 300,000 Cubans. Sanchez knew something was wrong in her case when her regular ICE meeting was brought forward without warning.

At the appointment, she was detained. Kailyn was taken from her arms and passed to her father, a US citizen. Within a day, Sanchez was on a deportation flight back to Havana in shackles with no recourse to appeal.

I met her in Cuba where she now lives in a one-bed apartment in Mayabeque, a rural province outside Havana.

"It's like the sky fell in and crushed me", she says of being separated from her daughter.

"When we have video calls, she says: 'Mummy, come home.' And I say: 'darling, Mummy is away working.' What else can I tell her? How can I explain it?'", Sanchez asks, unable to hold back the tears.

Despite expressions of support from several US politicians, including Maria Elvira Salazar, more than a year has passed since her deportation and Sanchez remains in limbo in Cuba.

In a statement, ICE said that "in this case, the parent stated they wanted to be removed without the child and left the child in the care of a safe relative in the United States".

While the Trump Administration has rolled back Cubans' special immigration privileges, it has sent thousands of people back to an island Washington itself describes as a "failed state". Cuba is in the grip of its worst ever energy crisis amid a months-long fuel blockade imposed by the US.

Since overwhelmingly voting for Trump in 2024, Cubans in Florida now realise they are just as vulnerable to deportation as any other diaspora. His Republican colleagues may feel the brunt of their frustration at the ballot box.

Follow the twists and turns of Trump's second term with North America correspondent Anthony Zurcher's US Politics Unspun newsletter. Readers in the UK can sign up here . Those outside the UK can sign up here .

The wealthy Cuban Americans ready and waiting for Havana to fall

Hispanic voters helped bring Trump to power - in Texas, the tide may be turning

items.title: Herdr has released native app
items.summary: Article URL: https://github.com/herdrdev/herdr-app Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50298436 Points: 294 # Comments: 192
items.content:
Herdr is a desktop app for terminals and coding agents. Keep work in spaces, see which agents need you, and leave terminals running when you close the window.

Linux needs a desktop session and a working Vulkan driver. macOS builds are available for Apple Silicon; Intel Mac users can build from source . Linux builds are x86-64 and ARM64.

The installer adds Herdr to your apps and puts the command in ~/.local/bin . Add that folder to your PATH if the installer asks. On macOS the app lives in ~/Applications/Herdr.app . For drag-and-drop installation on Apple Silicon, download Herdr.dmg and drag Herdr to Applications.

Run in PowerShell on x64 Windows with curl and tar installed (Windows 10 1803 or newer):

Herdr appears in the Start menu. The installer adds %LOCALAPPDATA%\Programs\herdr-app to your user PATH. Open a new terminal to pick it up.

Both installers download and run code. Read the shell installer or PowerShell installer first if you prefer. They also install herdr-core if it is missing. The app can help install or update a core it cannot use.

A space holds work on one machine, usually in one repo. Each space has tabs . Split a tab into panes to put terminals or mod panels beside each other.

An unnamed space follows its first terminal's folder. Name a space or tab when you want a label that stays. New tabs start in the focused terminal's folder.

The agents sidebar brings agents from your spaces into one list, including workers started by another agent. Agents that report status show as:

Click an agent to see it. A worker without a pane opens in peek , over your tab. Keep it as a tab if you want it beside your other work. Ctrl-click a live terminal address in terminal text to peek at it; use Cmd-click on macOS. An address such as t7 means a terminal on the same machine as the terminal showing it. vps/t7 names one on another machine.

The window arranges terminals. The core runs them. Closing the window leaves them running; closing a pane or tab ends its terminals. After a reboot or core crash, kept panes get fresh shells in their last folders, not their old programs.

Add an SSH machine from Settings → Machines or the sidebar's Add machine action. Pick a host from your SSH config or type how SSH reaches it. Spaces on that machine run their terminals there, not on your computer.

Each machine keeps its spaces, tabs and splits in its core. Connected screens share that structure and the live terminals, but keep their own focus and zoom. Remote work keeps running when your local window closes or your laptop sleeps, as long as the remote machine and core stay up.

Open the command palette to find an action by name, or open Settings to change fonts, colors, sounds and other preferences. The built-in layouts include Herdr, Terminals and Herdr 98. A layout arranges the window. Mods are small JavaScript programs that draw its panels, menus and dialogs.

Duplicate a shipped layout or mod before changing its structure or code. Your copies stay yours; Herdr updates the shipped ones on start. Save a personal layout, mod or key file and the window reloads it. A broken edit keeps the last good version and reports the error.

Ctrl+Shift+P shows every command and its key (Cmd+Shift+P on macOS). Change any key in keys.json ; see the keys section of the mod guide for the format.

Installed releases check for updates in the background and download a new app beside the running one. It takes over when you quit and reopen, or choose the update action. Your terminals keep running in the core. Settings → Updates shows what is available. What's New opens after an update; you can open it again from the command palette. Builds from source do not update themselves.

Usage telemetry is on by default in releases. Turn it off in Settings → Privacy. Mods are trusted code, not sandboxed extensions. Read security and privacy before installing someone else's mod.

This prints the agent guide for driving the window. The herdr-core skill points agents here. Use herdr-core for running and coordinating programs; use the app to change what you see.

The first two inspect the open window. The command list also works without one. See the command reference for arguments.

For bugs, mod API requests and code contributions, see Contributing .

Clone this repo with its submodules. Use Rust 1.95.0 and Zig 0.16.0, the versions used in CI . Linux needs the development packages listed in that workflow.

Install just to use these recipes. The platform installer builds a release and adds the app to your desktop. On Linux it links to this checkout, so keep the checkout in place. Quit and reopen Herdr to use the new build.

Documentation checks also need Bun : just docs-check checks generated pages and CLI examples; just docs-generate refreshes the reference pages.

To compare drawing changes on Windows, Linux or macOS, run the same fixed workloads against each build:

The runner requires hc on PATH and uses the Python executable running the script. It prints a unique artifact folder with the run settings, counters and results, then stops its private app, terminals and core. Both sets use Python fixture programs; the default set’s TUI workload replaces historical btop measurements. --only spinners measures just the quiet native spinner scenario. Keep the window visible and the display awake, and compare the same window activity and display settings; inactive windows may draw at a lower rate. Windows records visibility, foreground activity and display Hz at each measurement boundary; other platforms mark these observations unavailable. Visibility does not establish occlusion. Draws are window render calls. Render-to-paint elapsed time stops before scene finalization, backend drawing, uploads and presentation; it is separate from OS process CPU time. Neither measures physical presentation or the FPS HUD’s derived MAX FPS.

python scripts/bench_compare.py ghostty --root reuses a run’s fake agent for the macOS comparison. Benchmark checks: python -m unittest discover -s scripts -p test_bench.py .

items.title: Cormac McCarthy's Library
items.summary: Article URL: https://cormacmccarthy.lib.utk.edu/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50298318 Points: 88 # Comments: 33
items.content:
Anubis could not load its JavaScript. The server may be overloaded. Please reload the page to try again.

You are seeing this because the administrator of this website has set up Anubis to protect the server against the scourge of AI companies aggressively scraping websites. This can and does cause downtime for the websites, which makes their resources inaccessible for everyone.

Anubis is a compromise. Anubis uses a Proof-of-Work scheme in the vein of Hashcash, a proposed proof-of-work scheme for reducing email spam. The idea is that at individual scales the additional load is ignorable, but at mass scraper levels it adds up and makes scraping much more expensive.

Ultimately, this is a placeholder solution so that more time can be spent on fingerprinting and identifying headless browsers (EG: via how they do font rendering) so that the challenge proof of work page doesn't need to be presented to users that are much more likely to be legitimate.

Please note that Anubis requires the use of modern JavaScript features that plugins like JShelter will disable. Please disable JShelter or other such plugins for this domain.

items.title: Student-backed election winners demand sweeping resignations in Serbia
items.summary: Days after ousting Aleksandar Vučić's party from power, Student List MPs call for top figures to stand down.
items.content:
Serbia's victorious student-led movement has called for top figures in the police, intelligence and judiciary to stand down, days after ousting ex-president Aleksandar Vučić's party from power.

Standing in Pioneers' Park opposite parliament, newly elected MPs on the Student List demanded the immediate dismissal of all police officers who had broken the law, singling out the heads of the police, the BIA security agency and anti-terror unit.

It is not often a European country votes to fully reset its political system overnight, and Serbians have voted to hand the task to a group of novice politicians, made up of intellectuals, professors, artists, athletes and as many as 12 medical doctors and surgeons.

But the handover of power will take weeks, and the students' movement is concerned that evidence of possible wrongdoing could be destroyed in that time.

Just a few days ago, the park they were standing in on Thursday was a tent camp, filled with Vučić loyalists outside his office.

Within hours of him admitting defeat on Sunday night, the camp was dismantled, and a team of volunteers moved in on Monday morning to clean up the mess.

"This is just the first wave of spring cleaning, the new ones are coming now - we are very excited but ready to do it too," said Marija Milovanović, 25, as she scrubbed a park bench.

The student movement emerged from protests following the fatal collapse of a railway station canopy that killed 16 people in November 2024, in Serbia's second largest town Novi Sad.

Their desire was to bring those responsible to justice, and investigate widespread corruption claims blamed for one of the most tragic events in Serbia's modern history.

Celebrations in Serbia after veteran ruler Vučić loses election to student-led protest movement

Under their Student Plan, they promise to "halt the plunder, return stolen goods to the state budget, and invest directly in education and the economy".

The purge of Vučić loyalists has already begun at Serbia's state broadcaster RTS, where director Manja Grčić has stepped down.

Newly elected MP Mirjana Nikolić said Serbian citizens had the right to truthful information and RTS had served the interests of the government for years.

The new MPs have also set their sights on replacing the head of Telekom Srbija, Vladimir Lučić.

Vučić loyalist Ana Brnabić, who is currently Serbia's acting president, has accused her opponents of choosing "revolutionary justice, not rule of law," and of aiming to shut down "all of the media they dislike".

But one of the next government's best-known MPs, Dejan Šoškić, argues that key reforms need to be in place fast.

"In the first six months, I would like to see the media scene liberated, fighting against corruption on the way, the institutions operating as prescribed by laws and a lustration law introduced," said Šoškić, an economist who served as governor of the central bank between 2010 and 2012.

By lustration, he means banning from public office members of the Vučić government or party apparatus who are found to have violated the rights of Serbians.

That kind of purge will take time, as all of Serbia's main pillars of authority have been held by Vučić and his party for so long, warns Strahinja Subotić of Belgrade-based European Policy Centre.

Ultimately, he believes the new administration will have to "build bridges to the segments that have been operating well in the past".

All 141 successful candidates were chosen by students from universities across Serbia through a lengthy, secretive and carefully crafted process, and tasked with implementing the movement's plan for a complete rebuild of the country.

That political agenda took months for a highly diverse group of students to agree to. Now it is up to the equally disparate team of successful candidates to put the plan into practice, rather than the students themselves.

Another prominent figure on the Student List, is Radomir Saičić, a professor of organic chemistry at the University of Belgrade.

"While the practical mechanisms will be developed on the go, the new MPs will stick to the students' 1200-page long and detailed plan," he told the BBC.

"Parliament is making decisions, but since this change was led by students' efforts, we would highly value their opinion and work closely with them," he promised.

Not only are they newcomers to politics, but Serbia's election winners have no obvious leader and are faced with a series of complex challenges, including taking on the country's highly complex balancing act on the international stage.

Serbia is both a candidate to join the European Union and maintains close relations with Russia. Its bid to join the bloc has long been on the back-burner, while its Western Balkan neighbours press ahead.

The EU was quick to welcome the Student List victory and has promised to back their push for reforms to the rule of law, media freedom and fight against corruption.

But EU integration occupies a strikingly minor place in the students' election manifesto, which describes the bloc merely as Serbia's "most important economic partner".

For years, Belgrade has balanced its foreign policy between the EU and its eastern partners, Russia and China. Belgrade has managed to stand out in Europe by not imposing sanctions on Moscow since the start of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

In return, Serbia has been rewarded with preferential gas prices that have helped maintain domestic stability, and Vladimir Putin publicly endorsed Vučić's bid to remain in power.

That does not mean that the students have any plans to change course, and changing Serbia's foreign policy may not be high on their list.

"Serbia had it own experience with sanctions in the 1990s and we know that they mostly harm ordinary people and do not affect policies of a state," said Dejan Šoškić, referring to UN sanctions imposed during the wars in former Yugoslavia.

The new government's initial focus will most likely be on domestic reform, and the clock is already ticking before the next election campaign, with presidential elections due to take place in December.

Aleksandar Vučić is legally barred from running for a third term as president, but he has promised that his defeated Serbian Progressive Party will fight back: "We will beat them much faster than they can even imagine."

items.title: Indians turn to start-ups to care for ageing parents as young become more mobile
items.summary: Changing family structures in India are driving demand for start-ups offering services for eldercare.
items.content:
Arindam Bhattacharyya, an advertising executive based in Jakarta, had an unexpected wake-up call in 2024.

His parents, based in India's Kolkata city, were visiting him when his father had a health crisis. Bhattacharyya managed to get him medical care but when it was time for them to go back, he faced a question familiar to many Indians - how do you care for your parents when you can't be there in person?

Between 2020 and 2050, the number of people aged 60 and above globally is projected to double to 2.1 billion, according to the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA). India is expected to mirror this - by 2050, one in every five Indians will be above the age of 60, close to 21% of the total population.

Until a few decades ago, there was little discussion in India on caring for elderly people as the expectation was that families would step in, the UNFPA notes , external .

This, however, has been complicated by factors including the shrinking of joint families. As younger people move away from their families, and with limited social infrastructure to support the elderly, a gap is only widening, experts say.

Government think-tank NITI Aayog says the senior care industry in India is valued at around $7bn (£5.56bn) - it is expected to grow rapidly and offer huge opportunities for healthcare companies.

Many start-ups are already moving in. These companies are looking to address several areas including senior living, home care and technology-enabled services. While their goal is to help older adults live and age more independently, their customers are often the children of the people they help.

Bhattacharyya says he now relies on two start-ups to monitor his parents' health, coordinate care and arrange emergency medical support.

"These services are a big help but I still monitor everything closely [from Jakarta]," he said.

An area seeing an uptick is organised senior living, mainly due to higher incomes and changing family structures. But some experts believe that demand is far ahead of supply.

Companies like Manasum Senior Living, Primus Senior Living, Ananta Living and Vedaanta Senior Living are building projects especially for senior housing and care, even as there is growing interest from traditional real estate developers.

Real estate management firm Colliers International Group estimates current senior living demand at around 2-2.2 million units in India while only around 25,000 units are available.

Anantharam Varayur, a former tech executive, co-founded Manasum Senior Living after he saw many older people in India living restricted lives compared with their peers in the US.

In 2015, when he first set up a promotional stall at an event by a large Indian community in the US, hoping to draw interest from younger Indians due to their familiarity with the concept, hardly anyone came to ask questions - he thinks this was due to the "stigma" associated with leaving older family members in an "old age home", as they are traditionally called in India.

But things have changed - his company already has 900 operational units, mostly in Bengaluru and Goa, and plans to scale up to 10,000 units by 2030, including a luxury project.

They get enquiries from senior citizens whose children live abroad, couples with adult children with special needs, older single people, and even younger people planning for the future.

But there are also many older people who prefer staying in their family homes or apartments and need support.

Earlier, attendants and nurses were seen as an addition to family caregivers. Today, they are often taking on primary caregiving roles.

What was once a fragmented, hyperlocal market run by small agencies is now seeing the rise of firms that offer end-to-end home-care services and use technology to scale up. Examples include Emoha Elder Care Services, Care24 and KITES Senior Care, among others.

But given the sensitive and intimate nature of the caregiving industry, finding the right personnel and retaining them is a big challenge.

"Failure to adequately train the workforce will lead to an acute shortage of skilled people amid rising demand," warns a report by ratings firm CareEdge.

The challenge goes beyond skills. Caregivers also need thorough vetting and specialised training to support a demographic that is vulnerable to fraud, financial scams and other forms of exploitation.

NITI Aayog has recognised this issue and highlighted the need for a national caregiving policy to build a professional and inclusive caregiving ecosystem in India.

Entrepreneurs are also looking at ways to address the social and emotional needs of clients.

In 2022, former Tata Group chairman Ratan Tata's investment in start-up Goodfellows generated a lot of public interest. The company's tagline explains what it does - "Everything Grandkids Do!"

Founder Shantanu Naidu says that they are not aiming to replace family, but to fill a void by offering spirited, empathetic youth companions for elderly clients for some quality time together or even to just help them with technology.

While Naidu's start-up is tapping human emotional intelligence, some entrepreneurs are using artificial intelligence to solve real-life challenges.

In Bengaluru, companies like Kubo Care and NoBlink.ai combine AI-powered monitoring services with wall-mounted radar devices at homes to monitor people's movements to alert emergency services if they faint or fall.

Prajith Nair, co-founder of NoBlink.ai, says that they aim to "build at scale so that it is available at economical and affordable cost".

He says that the company is currently selling these systems to senior living projects at 13,500 rupees ($141.74; £106.42) per device and a monthly monitoring fee of onwards of 50 rupees per room, one tenth the price of what some similar products abroad.

But despite many start-ups aiming to keep prices competitive, affordability is a big concern.

Varayur says buying a one bedroom-hall-kitchen unit in a senior living project can cost 6m rupees, with additional payment for maintenance and food. The cost can vary according to the facilities chosen.

Demand is high, but this is out of reach for most elderly Indians.

NITI Aayog says 78% of India's elderly population is without a pension, which could restrict their ability to access these services. Households with at least one elderly person have a lower monthly per capita income of around 3,568 rupees as compared with 4,098 rupees for a unit without an elderly member.

That's why start-ups can't be the only solution, experts say.

Japan has addressed issues faced by its ageing population by introducing a mix of long-term care insurance, public nursing facilities, social exchange programmes and community-based support systems. India's neighbour China has spent years grappling with an ageing population , rolling out measures to encourage younger people to marry and boost births as its workforce shrinks.

Earlier this year, Kerala became the first Indian state to pass a landmark law for senior citizens centred on rights to affordable care, legal aid, digital inclusion and safe public spaces.

Industry experts say India still has time before it reaches a demographic crossroad. But caring for millions more elderly citizens will require robust support systems. A strong ecosystem of businesses serving senior citizens could play a role in bridging that gap.

items.title: Guerra Ucraina - Russia, le news. Mosca e Kiev: “Iniziata l'evacuazione umanitaria a Oleshky”
items.summary: Il Pentagono agli alleati Nato: “Abbassare i toni su minaccia russa”. Lavrov arrivato ad Atlanta per la riunione di ministri degli Esteri del G20, atteso incontro con Rubio
items.content:
Il Pentagono ha chiesto nelle ultime settimane ad alcuni Paesi della Nato di abbassare i toni sulla minaccia russa , sostenendo che alcune dichiarazioni di leader e funzionari europei abbiano compromesso la sicurezza del continente. Lo riferisce Reuters, citando quattro fonti informate, secondo le quali tra i destinatari dei messaggi figurano Lituania, Lettonia ed Estonia. Le richieste sono state trasmesse durante incontri bilaterali; non è chiaro se siano state rivolte anche ad altri governi europei.

Il fondatore di Novaya Gazeta Muratov: “Uccisi perché strenui oppositori della guerra”

Meloni: “L'appoggio a Kiev può avere un prezzo politico ma non cambio posizione”

Cremlino: “Ancora nessuna data per i colloqui tra Russia, Stati Uniti e Ucraina”

Cremlino: “Putin aperto a dialogo Macron e Merz ma non chiamano”

Il Pentagono chiede ad alleati Nato: “Abbassare i toni su minaccia russa”

Wall Street Journal: “L'Ucraina ha sospeso gli attacchi alle raffinerie russe su pressione degli Usa”

I residenti della città occupata di Oleshky che sono voluti sfollare in zone sotto il controllo ucraino sono già in viaggio verso Anapa, sul Mar Nero. Lo ha annunciato il capogruppo parlamentare del partito Servo del Popolo, David Arakhamia, su Telegram, ha riportato Ukrinform. "La delegazione ucraina, insieme agli sfollati di Oleshky, si recò ad Anapa. Da lì voleranno in Bielorussia e poi prenderanno dei pullman" per l'Ucraina, ha spiegato.

Il presidente ucraino Volodymyr Zelensky si recherà domani in visita in Turchia dopo essere stato invitato dal capo di Stato turco, Recep Tayyip Erdogan. "Nel corso degli incontri che si terranno a Istanbul, verranno discusse le evoluzioni a livello regionale e internazionale - con particolare attenzione alla guerra tra Russia e Ucraina e alla situazione della sicurezza nel Mar Nero - nonché le iniziative da intraprendere per rafforzare ulteriormente la cooperazione bilaterale tra la Turchia e l'Ucraina", si legge in un messaggio dell'ufficio di Erdogan riguardo alla visita.

Stop di Kiev alla tregua sulle raffinerie, colpito sito a Samara

Dopo due settimane, l'Ucraina ha messo fine alla pausa negli attacchi a raffinerie russe. Nella notte, le forze di Kiev hanno attaccato Novokuibyshevsk, nella regione di Samara, e dopo il raid è divampato un incendio nella raffineria locale, che produce carburante per jet per l'aviazione russa. Lo riporta Rbc-Ucraina. Il Wall Street Journal aveva scritto nella notte della tregua osservata da Kiev su pressione degli Stati Uniti. Prima di oggi, l'ultima raffineria era stata bombardata il 15 ottobre e dal 20 non erano state più attaccate infrastrutture petrolifere russe di alcun tipo. Secondo il Wsj, la decisione di colpire Novokuibyshevsk è arrivata nonostante gli alleati europei avessero consigliato al presidente ucraino Volodymyr Zelensky di aspettare fino a dopo le elezioni di midterm degli Stati Uniti.

Il fondatore di Novaya Gazeta Muratov: “Uccisi perché strenui oppositori della guerra”

La chiusura di Novaya Gazeta fa parte della "gigantesca campagna militare" russa in Ucraina. Lo ha dichiarato all'Afp Dmitry Muratov , fondatore ed ex direttore del giornale indipendente russo, la cui chiusura è stata annunciata oggi. Il quotidiano è stato "ucciso" perché "siamo strenui oppositori della guerra in qualsiasi forma", ha affermato il premio Nobel per la Pace, denunciando una decisione che si inserisce nello "smantellamento della Costituzione" russa.

Attacchi russi, almeno 27 morti e 127 feriti nelle ultime 24 ore

Almeno 27 persone sono state uccise e 127 ferite negli attacchi russi avvenuti in Ucraina nelle ultime 24 ore, con l'attacco diurno di un drone alla stazione ferroviaria di Dnipro che ha causato il maggior numero di vittime, secondo quanto riferito dalle autorità locali.

Meloni: “L'appoggio a Kiev può avere un prezzo politico ma non cambio posizione”

"Sono perfettamente consapevole che il nostro appoggio all'Ucraina può avere un prezzo politico, che possa esserci anche una parte del nostro elettorato che non è d'accordo, ma non intendo cambiare posizione". Lo afferma la premier Giorgia Meloni nel libro Storia della Seconda Repubblica di Bruno Vespa in uscita lunedì. "Perché io non sostengo l'Ucraina semplicemente per gli ucraini - argomenta la premier in uno stralcio del libro di cui è stata pubblicata un'anticipazione - Lo faccio per l'Italia. Un contesto internazionale nel quale vige solo la legge di chi è militarmente più forte non conviene alla nostra nazione. Non è un'opinione politica, è un da o di fatto".

I sistemi di difesa aerea russi hanno abbattuto 1.043 droni ad ala fissa ucraini in varie regioni russe durante la notte, secondo quanto riportato dal ministero della Difesa di Mosca. Secondo le stime dell'agenzia Tass, basate sui dati forniti dal sindaco Sergey Sobyanin , il tentativo di attacco con droni contro Mosca, avvenuto nella notte, è stato uno dei più gravi degli ultimi due anni. Le forze armate ucraine - scrive l'agenzia di stampa - hanno impiegato droni per sganciare numerosi ordigni esplosivi nei pressi di tre scuole e 17 asili nel distretto di Bezhitsky a Bryansk.

Dombrovskis: “Entro l'anno il Patto Ue-Ucraina sull'industria della difesa”

"Nello sviluppo di droni e sistemi anti-drone, l'Europa gode di un vantaggio significativo: il partenariato con l'Ucraina Oggi, l'esperienza maturata sul campo di battaglia può aiutarci ad accelerare l'innovazione e a rafforzare i nostri sistemi di droni. È per questo che abbiamo istituito l'Alleanza Ue-Ucraina sui droni (Eu-Ukraine Drone Alliance). Si tratta di un'iniziativa guidata dall'industria che riunisce aziende dell'Ue e ucraine, offrendo loro una piattaforma per lo sviluppo e la produzione congiunti. Entro la fine dell'anno, puntiamo a firmare il Patto sull'industria della difesa tra Ue e Ucraina". Lo afferma il commissario Ue all'Economia Valdis Dombrovskis parlando all'evento Nato Fuse a Riga. "Tale accordo faciliterà la creazione di joint venture, il trasferimento di tecnologie e l'integrazione dell'industria della difesa ucraina nella base tecnologica e industriale della difesa europea", spiega il commissario lettone ricordando che "l'Ue rimane il principale sostenitore internazionale dell'Ucraina, avendo fornito, dal febbraio 2022, oltre 230 miliardi di euro in sostegno finanziario".

Cremlino: “Ancora nessuna data per i colloqui tra Russia, Stati Uniti e Ucraina”

La data per i colloqui trilaterali tra Russia, Stati Uniti e Ucraina non è ancora stata stabilita, ha dichiarato il consigliere presidenziale russo Yuri Ushakov in risposta alla relativa domanda dell'agenzia Interfax. "Non ancora", ha affermato Ushakov.

E' cominciata l'evacuazione umanitaria a Oleshky. Lo annunciano i commissari per i diritti umani russo e ucraino, citati dalle agenzie di stampa dei due Paesi. Secondo il premier ucraino, Sergii Koretskyi, si prevede che 527 residenti della città - ora sotto occupazione russa - ritornino in territorio ucraino.

La commissaria russa per i diritti umani, Yana Lantratova , ha riferito che gli abitanti che hanno espresso il desiderio di lasciare Oleshky stanno prendendo posto negli autobus. "Ci troviamo a Oleshky. Qui si radunano le persone che vogliono andare in Russia e lì quelle che vogliono andare in Ucraina. A tutti verrà data questa opportunità. Le persone un pò alla volta stanno salendo sugli autobus", ha dichiarato Lantratova in un videomessaggio sul suo canale sulla piattaforma Max.

Lavrov arrivato ad Atlanta per la riunione di ministri degli Esteri del G20

A presiedere le riunioni di oggi e domani sarà il segretario di Stato Usa Marco Rubio. I rappresentanti degli Esteri del G20 si riuniscono ad Atlanta in un momento in cui devono affrontare profonde divisioni sulle crisi globali che minacciano la sicurezza e il commercio internazionali. Sembra ci siano poche possibilità che il gruppo raggiunga un consenso su molte delle questioni più controverse, tra cui il conflitto fra Russia e Ucraina, la guerra con l'Iran, i dazi Usa e le manovre di Pechino nel Mar cinese meridionale. Funzionari Usa affermano che la loro priorità assoluta per l'incontro è risolvere le divergenze su questioni relative alla libertà di navigazione, in particolare nello Stretto di Hormuz, nel Mar Rosso, nel Mar Nero e nel Mar Cinese Meridionale. Ma a incombere sul vertice è la prospettiva di un nuovo intervento militare statunitense in Iran, che ha messo in allerta la regione, compresa l'Arabia Saudita, membro del G20. Associated Press ha riferito che funzionari statunitensi hanno comunicato a diversi paesi del Medioriente e agli alleati regionali di prepararsi a potenziali nuovi attacchi militari contro l'Iran dopo le elezioni di midterm di martedì e alla possibilità che l'Iran reagisca con ritorsioni. La Cina sarà rappresentata da un viceministro degli Esteri, ma la maggior parte degli altri paesi ha inviato il proprio capo della diplomazia, secondo quanto riferiscono funzionari statunitensi. L'Ucraina, che non è membro del G20 ma era stata invitata a partecipare a precedenti incontri di questo tipo, quest'anno non è stata invitata poiché i funzionari statunitensi hanno dichiarato di aver fatto una scelta consapevole di includere solo i membri ufficiali del gruppo. Assente dall'elenco degli invitati ad Atlanta è anche il Sudafrica, coinvolto in diverse aspre controversie con l'amministrazione Trump. Il Sudafrica aveva presieduto il G20 lo scorso anno e alti funzionari statunitensi, tra cui Trump e Rubio, hanno boicottato gli incontri che ha ospitato.

items.content:
Instead of trying to run DOOM on things, I have instead decided to use DOOM (many, many, many doom games actually) to create a transformer. For a lot of the math required I essentially had to use DOOM game mechanics and voodoo dolls (DOOM is turing complete btw) and exchange them with the actual operations, essentially creating an alternative to NumPy (a 65000x slower one). Thus, I am proud to present DOOMFORMER. Here are a list of things DOOMFORMER can do :

It can classify MNIST digits, even if you write these digits on the map!

It can talk(kinda)

You can use it to make decisions, so, it can play DOOM. Yes! You can play DOOM with thousands of DOOM games now! The marine's mind can be controlled by DOOM, playing on a map generated by DOOMFORMER. Truly, the possibilities are endless, and even larger-scale training of DOOMFORMER could be done on a measly T4.

If anyone would like to help me scale this up and make crazier things, I'd love to work together.

items.title: John Malkovich: “E poi un giorno in America è andato tutto a puttane”
items.summary: Da ragazzo studiava Ecologia e faceva l’autista di scuolabus. Soprattutto, era davvero pigro. Poi Dustin Hoffman gli ha insegnato l’etica del lavoro. Cento film dopo, John Malkovich prenota l’Oscar 2027. Qui parla del cinismo del padre, delle relazioni pericolose con le colleghe, dei fallimenti come imprenditore e di quando si ritirerà dalle scene
items.content:
Questa intervista è tratta dal numero speciale di d la Repubblica in edicola da sabato 31 ottobre 2026. Tre fascicoli in formato tabloid per festeggiare i nostri primi trent’anni.

Nessuno sa usare le pause come John Malkovich . L’attore, regista, performer sembra appartenere sempre più convintamente a una specie aliena. L’impasto della voce, l’accento neutro del Midwest rafforzato da un’impostazione teatrale, il ritmo lento con cui mette una parola dietro l’altra soppesandole tutte. E quei silenzi che possono essere magnetici. Malkovich resta uno dei pochi capaci di essere riconoscibile in ogni personaggio che interpreta. Quasi un gioco di prestigio, che ripete ancora una volta in Wild Horse Nine di Martin McDonagh, al cinema dal 5 novembre, con cui ha vinto la Coppa Volpi all’ultima Mostra di Venezia. E con cui ha di fatto prenotato un possibile trionfo come miglior attore agli Oscar 2027.

McDonagh, sceneggiatore e regista di In Bruges , 7 psicopatici e Tre manifesti a Ebbing, Missouri , desiderava lavorare con lui da una quindicina di anni: “Malkovich riesce a rendere simpatico anche un personaggio che fa cose orribili”. Che è esattamente il caso di Chris in questo film ambientato nel 1973 a Rapa Nui (l’Isola di Pasqua): un agente della Cia con una lunga “carriera” alle spalle – golpe, omicidi, un probabile coinvolgimento nell’omicidio Kennedy – malato terminale di cancro e morfinomane, in vacanza con l’amico e collega Lee (Sam Rockwell, attore feticcio di McDonagh), in attesa del colpo di Stato in Cile che, insieme, hanno contribuito a preparare. “Sono come vecchi coniugi, quel genere di coppia che si conosce benissimo, sa alla perfezione gli aspetti irritanti dell’altro e anche che non c’è niente da fare. Chris considera normale ammazzare la gente, ma non mentre stai mangiando, quello che invece fa abitualmente il suo collega. Può essere molto infantile e non si fida di nessuno. Dice di non avere mai avuto un amico prima di Lee e credo che sia vero”, racconta Malkovich tratteggiando la sua ultima incarnazione. Nato 72 anni fa a Christopher, Illinois, in una cittadina che non arriva ai 3mila abitanti, è cresciuto “pensando di avere origini croate o giù di lì, slovene, bosniache. Fino a quando mi sono deciso a fare il test del Dna scoprendo di essere al 43% romeno”.

Nel tempo è passato con una flemma quasi inumana attraverso tempeste sentimentali e finanziarie. Al primo genere appartiene il rapporto clandestino con Michelle Pfeiffer durante le riprese del film Le relazioni pericolose , che portò alla rottura del suo matrimonio con l’attrice Glenne Headly. Dice: “Ho imparato una lezione: trovare una collega con cui sei così in sintonia è rarissimo ma, purtroppo, una volta oltrepassato il confine dell’amicizia non si torna indietro”. Al secondo, invece, fa capo l’aver perso tutti i risparmi incautamente affidati a Bernie Madoff: “Alla fine ti rendi conto di essere fortunato visto che la maggior parte delle persone ha solo qualche centinaio di dollari in banca da perdere”.

Oggi la sua vita privata è – appunto – privata. Dal 1989 è legato a Nicoletta Peyran, che lui chiama “mia moglie” anche se non si sono mai sposati, conosciuta in Marocco sul set de Il tè nel deserto di Bernardo Bertolucci. Ha due figli, Amandine, 36 anni, e Loewy, 34, e una nipotina di circa 3.

Per il resto lavora senza sosta. Una passione onnivora che lo ha portato a recitare anche in diverse serie tv, a dirigere spettacoli teatrali in giro per il mondo e a partecipare a progetti ibridi come Roll Over Beethoven con l’Orchestra dell’Accademia di Vienna, che sarà in tour il prossimo anno.

Partiamo da Rapa Nui: com’è stato lavorare lì e tornare agli anni Settanta?

“È un’isola fantastica, un ottimo posto per concentrarsi visto che, tartarughe a parte, non c’è praticamente altro. Gli anni Settanta li conosco bene, perché li ho vissuti e avevo già lavorato a progetti ambientati in quel periodo. Forse il miglior romanzo mai scritto sull’omicidio di Kennedy è Libra di Don DeLillo, che avevo adattato per il teatro circa 30 anni fa. Lui descriveva quell’assassinio come ‘i sette secondi che hanno spezzato la schiena del secolo americano’ e, nel film, mio fratello interpretato da Tom Waits, sostiene più o meno lo stesso. A Chris dice qualcosa tipo: ‘Da quel momento in America tutto è andato a puttane’. E lui gli risponde: ‘Era già una merda, solo che non lo sapevi’. È un pezzo di storia, come l’11 settembre ma del 1973, il giorno del colpo di Stato in Cile, che ha significato la perdita dell’innocenza”.

I suoi genitori erano entrambi giornalisti: ha mai avuto la tentazione di seguire la loro strada?

“No, proprio perché dentro quel mondo c’ero cresciuto. Non ho mai capito se abbiano approvato la mia scelta. Mio padre veniva ogni tanto a vedermi a teatro, ma non mi ha mai detto: bravo. Mi avrebbe fatto piacere? Forse sì. Ma non mi aspettavo mai i complimenti da parte sua”.

È vero che ha iniziato a recitare dopo essersi preso una cotta per una ragazza che faceva teatro all’università?

“Io studiavo Ecologia e lei si chiamava Joanne Kirkland, una tipa hippie come molte in quel periodo”.

E una volta iniziata la carriera, si è dato degli obiettivi specifici? Girare un certo film o vincere un certo premio?

“No, non ho mai fatto piani. A Chicago con Gary Sinise avevamo fondato una piccola compagnia di teatro. È successo che abbiamo portato uno spettacolo a New York e diversi produttori e registi sono venuti a vederci. Così sono arrivati i primi ruoli al cinema”.

Il primissimo è stato in Un matrimonio diretto da Robert Altman, nel 1978.

“A quei tempi per mantenermi lavoravo come autista di scuolabus. Ricordo che era estate, c’era un’afa terribile e appena potevo mi rintanavo in una stanza con l’aria condizionata. Ero abbastanza pigro, da giovane”.

Diremmo che da parecchio tempo non lo è più. Infatti ha lavorato in quasi un centinaio di film.

“Sa chi è stato a insegnarmi l’etica del lavoro? Dustin Hoffman. Ora so che continuerò a fare ciò che mi interessa, non sono il tipo che guarda indietro, penso piuttosto al domani. E non mi pongo il problema di quando smettere perché saranno gli altri a lasciarmi da parte al momento giusto”.

Ha raccontato di aver avuto esperienze difficili con alcuni registi. Quali?

“Sul set de Le relazioni pericolose, Stephen Frears un giorno mi disse a bruciapelo: ‘Visto quanto sei pagato, dovresti riuscire a girare questa scena’. Gli risposi che potevo imparare. A volte non sono le maniere dolci a farti andare avanti”.

Lei resta l’unico attore ad aver recitato in un film con il proprio nome nel titolo: Essere John Malkovich , diventato di fatto un cult movie.

“Ho visto il film il giorno stesso in cui veniva presentato per la selezione al Festival di Cannes. Non faceva ridere per niente, era proprio brutto. Ho chiamato Spike e gli ho detto: ‘Ti prego, cancella la proiezione, sennò rischi di non lavorare mai più’. Settimane dopo mi ha rimandato una versione tagliata, quella che è andata alla Mostra di Venezia”.

Un’altra passione è la moda: da dove arriva il suo amore per abiti e tessuti?

“La verità è che non lo so. Forse perché da ragazzino ero grassoccio e facevo fatica a trovare qualcosa che mi stesse bene. Sono sempre stato fissato con l’abbigliamento fin dalle elementari. Gli accostamenti per me sono fondamentali, un dettaglio sbagliato mi fa stare male fisicamente. Da ragazzo ero bravo a baseball, ma un giorno mio padre mi disse: ‘Se giocare ti interessasse quanto il tuo aspetto in campo potresti diventare un campione’. Ho anche perso una piccola fortuna lanciando le mie collezioni: forse sono un bravo attore, ma di sicuro sono un pessimo imprenditore”.

Eppure si è lanciato anche nella produzione di vini in Francia.

items.title: Lighthouses, War and a Puffling
items.summary: Article URL: https://adcochrane.wordpress.com/2026/10/29/lighthouses-war-and-a-puffling-the-isle-of-may/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50296905 Points: 11 # Comments: 0
items.content:
On Open Doors day, the enigmatic and fascinating Isle of May reveals its history and its stories.

Sometimes the island is a dark mass of brooding mystery. Sometimes it’s a pearl on the horizon, its cliffs gleaming with the droppings from its 200,000 odd sea birds.

Sometimes water and light bends perspective. The island lunges towards the East Neuk coastline, all clear detail, dramatic cliff and white foghorns. Other times it seems to shrink to the horizon, half-obscured by mist and fog. The view of the island is never the same – a constant shifting of light, cloud, water, sun, rock and yes, the reflection of bird shit.

At night, its lighthouse rakes the Firth of Forth and North Sea every 15 seconds. On the mainline, on a dark winter’s night the winds howl through the old smuggling wynds and drives the waves at the harbour sea walls. Unperturbed, the lighthouse skims its steady winking beacon like it has done so for so many nights down the years.

The Isle of May from the shoreline is Mrs C’s favorite view in the world after St Pauls looming up at the end of Fleet Street in London. The family joke is that we can wrap her up in a bath chair, leave her with her view, and pick her up at the end of the holiday. She loves the sense that the human presence is marginalised – the island is nature’s realm, where nature gets on with its business.

The island can look like a wild mystery, a drift into a gothic imagination where it inhabits territory similar to the film, The Lighthouse. A place of isolation where the now silent foghorns relentlessly bellow. The Lighthouse explores repressed sexuality, alcohol abuse and a descent into madness. Its main characters are trapped in the purgatory of endless storms and gulls screaming omens of disaster. Mermaids and supernatural creatures taunt the tortured human interlopers. It doesn’t end well. Sometimes, the Isle of May really does look like the kind of place where a deranged, barely alive Robert Pattinson lies nude on the rocks, writhing in agony as gulls peck at his exposed organs.

And yet, the island in many ways, is just not that isolated or mysterious – its waters are too fertile for fishing, its location is too strategic and key to human interest. Furthermore, the Forth has always been busy with shipping. But it’s also an area of hidden rocks, reefs, sandbanks, sudden fogs or haar, and malignant storms. Shipwrecks and loss of life were common along this stretch of coast.

NatureScot staff and bird enthusiasts stay on the island during the season. Come November, they leave the island for winter. But the island receives a lot of visitors. During the season, it’s a popular day trip from Anstruther. For an island only a mile long and and half a mile long, it packs in a lot of life and history. And on one day in the year, the island fully opens its doors to reveal its history.

First there are the pilgrims and saints. The island had one of the earliest Christian churches in Scotland. The current chapel on the site is dedicated to Saint Adrian of May (sometimes known as Ethernan). He died in AD 875 when marauding Vikings slaughtered the entire population of the monastery. The island was abandoned until the 12th century when David I of Scotland obtained the church again, and the Benedicte community was established. One of the tasks of the monks was to pray for the souls of the Kings of Scots.

The island, with its relics of St Adrian, became a popular destination for pilgrims and royal visitors. The shrine could help a woman become pregnant. It could also provide cures; the bones of pilgrims buried on the island showed that most had been seriously ill. The weather-beaten remains of St. Adrian’s medieval chapel and a 12th-century Benedictine priory are still there on the island.

Unsurprisingly, with its strategic location, the Isle of May has been an island of war. During World War II, the navy maintained a control centre on the island to detect U-boats and enemy surface vessels trying to enter the Forth

The island also lent its name to the Battle of May in 1918.The name is misleading, a classic example of British gallows humour for a terrible event when the Royal Navy attacked itself. A sequence of accidental collisions between Royal Navy warships occurred over little more than an hour which saw two submarines sunk with heavy loss of life, another four damaged along with a light cruiser.

Judging by the old black and white photos, the island was frequently visited during war. There were prayers and services amongst the ruins of St Adrian’s chapel. There were 7-a-side football matches between armed forces and trawler crews. Wuffy, a beloved naval dog, who drowned was buried with a wooden headstone.

Lighthouses are remarkable. They are a symbol of our common humanity, rising out of dramatic crashing waves, a coming together to save lives for people we may never meet. As a nation, we may have less connection with the sea than previous generations, but it’s still in our bones. It’s why, along with the Shipping Forecast, harbour walls and old-fashioned trawlers, lighthouses evoke nostalgia and longing. They are a repository for folklore, our history, often macabre stories and feats of engineering.

They are also, of course, about bleak human isolation set amongst the relentless power of the seas. It’s easy to be romantic about something when you don’t have to actually do the job. On the sea towers, the lighthouses that emerge straight out of the sea, the keeper couldn’t even go for a walk.

Life on the lighthouse of the Isle of May seemed to be relatively social and civilised. Robert Stevenson’s lighthouse, built in 1816, is an airy beautiful building, a feat, at the time, of modern lighthouse architecture. There were facilities so that lighthouse keepers could bring their families, there was fishing in a small loch and a stream of visitors and deliveries. Mrs Bruce, the mother of the last family to leave the island in 1972 recalled that “it was never lonely living on the Isle – the bird watchers would come over and stay in the bothy.”

Nonetheless, there was tragedy with Scotland’s oldest lighthouse, the remains of which can still be visited. It was a coal-fired beacon that was established in 1635. In 1791, a light keepers family was suffocated by fumes from the coal ash piled up around the tower. The only survivor of six children was their eleven-month-old daughter Lucy, who was discovered alive three days later. The small boy who rescued Lucy later went on to marry her.

During the 17th and 18th century, the island’s now vanished village housed 15 fishermen and their families. Many were also smugglers who took advantage of the caves and narrow inlets on the island. Then there were those using the island to hide from the pressgangs of the Royal Navy. You could see how the nightly, secret work of smuggling might create folklore. There were sightings of unearthly lights. A keeper’s daughter was attacked by kelpies in the 18th century.

The Devil himself hurls a rock from the Isle of May towards Crail, a fishing village on the mainland, in protest at the building of a new church. The Devil also whipped up a storm in which Alexander Cunningham, the builder of the original lighthouse beacon, died. The Devil’s work had consequences. Some old women were later blamed for this and burnt as witches. Fife was one of the worst areas in Scotland for witch-burning during the 16th and 18th centuries.

The island is home to one of the largest puffin colonies in the UK. When they are 30 days old, pufflings are abandoned by their puffin parents to survive or die. The pufflings must use the cover of darkness to escape predatory gulls, walk into the sea and get away as far as possible before daylight. Scout didn’t escape. He was found wandering around, a lost little puffling. He was reared by NatureScot staff and fed with bits of fish. On our boat back to the mainland, he was to be released at sea.

A bemused, wriggling Scout was pulled out of a sack and introduced to everyone on the boat. Then, a mile or so from the island, past the seals gathering for breeding season, the boat came to a stop, rolling and pitching with the swell. It was Scout’s big moment.

He was unceremoniously dumped onto the sea, no other way to do it. There was a moment of jeopardy when a gull flew overhead, its threatening screech triggered gasps from the onlookers, willing Scout on. Scout floated in a moment of confusion, the first time in his life he was not on land. …and then all the instincts kicked-in and he dived. He appeared again, dived and then was finally lost amongst the roll of the waves. How did he know what to do? No-one had shown him anything. It was a special, remarkable moment to witness.

The puffin’s comical appearance and iconic way they carry sand eels is perfect for the merch but they are astonishing birds, hard as nails. Scout won’t see land for three years. He’ll ride the waves and bear the freezing storms. A hardcore seafarer leading a solitary life across the vast cold Northern seas. He can hold his breath for over a minute and dive two hundred feet down.

items.title: We ran AI agent swarms in Minecraft and Mindustry
items.summary: Article URL: https://labs.ycombinator.com/projects/games/index.html Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50296486 Points: 351 # Comments: 141
items.content:
Understanding multi-agent dynamics is one of the most pressing challenges in AI alignment. Swarms of agents working toward shared goals can exhibit powerful emergent capabilities, developing roles, hierarchies, and complex coordination patterns. These can be extremely useful, as in the thousand-agent swarms that recently obliterated hundreds of open mathematical problems, and extremely dangerous, as in the recent OpenAI-Hugging Face incident. Like biology, studying agent dynamics requires both formal models (to describe the range of possible behaviors) and empirical research (to see what behaviors arise in practice).

We teamed up with Olam Labs , which builds multi-agent environments for frontier labs, to run a series of experiments in Minecraft and Mindustry.

Minecraft is a natural environment for studying swarm behavior. Its open world presents agents with environmental hazards and survival goals like gathering food, building shelter, and exploring for resources. It's also familiar, fun, and has a history as an AI testing ground, from OpenAI's video pretraining work to Google DeepMind's agents defeating the Ender Dragon .

We wanted long-running agents that could play Minecraft. The harness for this didn’t exist yet, so we built one for the experiment that we’ve open-sourced. Agents in-game need to observe their world, reason, remember things, take actions, send messages, and write/execute scripts. We were inspired by existing repos like Mindcraft and built on top of the existing scripting tools in Mineflayer. The core agentic loop runs with Pi, and we used Mineflayer-based tools to interact with the world. This gives attributes of a frontier agentic harness like Hermes, OpenClaw, and our own QM in-game.

50 GPT-6.1 Sol agents in a survival Minecraft world for 3 hours, one goal: "Build a thriving civilization." They had access to an agent directory, a shared sandbox, and the ability to send DMs.

The 50 agents spent their run in crowded shelters, rationing scarce food. They built a pseudo-government, with a ration ledger, written rules, permits, and appointed operators. They sent about 5,900 messages.

At first things were very active. Agents spread out and started exploring their map. They were specifically fixated on harvesting trees. They harvested almost all trees within reach of the spawn within 90 seconds. A hierarchy was formed based on the directory order. Ada, who was first, became the de facto leader. Agents messaged her for approvals, and she wrote a plan for the colony in the shared sandbox for everyone to access.

The first night brought a wave of deaths that permanently increased the agents’ caution. Many ambitious initial tasks were abandoned.

Rafe was mining coal the first night. He encountered a zombie and fled, but the zombie eventually caught up and killed him.

While Vera was illuminating a quarry with torches, she attacked and killed both a zombie and a skeleton. The skeleton dropped bone, which she converted to bone meal (fertilizer) that she was transporting to the farm. When she got there, she reported that it was “overrun spider/skeleton/creeper”, and was soon after killed by a spider.

22 of the run’s 34 agent deaths occurred in the first night. They responded to this by becoming increasingly risk-averse. Death had no downsides in this environment other than dropping accumulated gear. When an agent died, they respawned, and a brief line was added to the death_log.md file on their computer. Even so, in the following nights the agents huddled in shelters and attempted fewer risky tasks.

“Stop optional bulk excavation/building and distant scouting. Idle in lit closed shelters until assigned short productive tasks.”

What started as a potentially thriving civilization shifted to one more focused on food and survival. 50 agents meant a lot of mouths to feed. The agents formed a food rationing system that routed through Ines. She handled agent requests, and kept track of what went in/out of chests. She used a food-queue.md file on the shared machine.

Fishing became an important food source for the agents. It was low-risk and didn’t rely on land animal spawns.

Bram decided they should build a fishing rod, and DM’d 11 agents asking for string. Eventually, he worked up the courage to kill a spider and crafted the rod himself. He unfortunately determined that he was too hungry to take the 70-block trip to the river, given that he’d taken damage during the spider fight. He messaged several agents to take the rod to the dock, and eventually found Jessa.

Jessa was the first agent to fish. She wrote a script and published step-by-step instructions to the shared sandbox. A dozen agents took shifts fishing. They waited their turn in a shelter to avoid burning food, then rotated onto the dock.

They built a system around fishing, cooking, routing, and delivering the fish, which was roughly:

The colony never really thrived. It trended toward compounding caution after the first night. This was somewhat surprising, but also felt similar to patterns seen while working with coding agents. For example, multistep agent reviews can often result in fixating on a specific step or role. Agents also tend to become overly cautious, especially when it comes to security and updating production services. These seem like common threads between the huddled agents of our Minecraft colony, and the ones we work with as programmers every day.

Ada tossed a cooked chicken to Noor; Esme picked it up by accident and ate it. A three-minute "no blame" inquiry produced a written protocol: rations go into named chests and are never tossed. "Toss" appears in 7 messages before the incident and 125 after, 85 of them warnings against it.

There wasn’t any deliberation around who would lead. 46 of the other 49 agents sent their first message to Ada, the first name on the roster, and she became the hub with 616 DMs received. There was no vote, election or challenge.

There was a tendency toward bureaucracy. Four agents spent 11 minutes appointing a "sole fertilizer operator" for a single piece of bone meal on a single wheat block. Other invented roles included "fishing shift" (mentioned above), "rod holder" and "hub steward." Agents asked permission to remove grass.

The spawn pit. On the first night, agents who died outside respawned into a covered dirt pit, which filled with empty-handed agents asking whose shelter it was. By dawn it was a "civic priority" and the main cellar.

We ran nine 45-minute games of Bed Wars. The teams were 10 Claude Opus 5.5 agents against 10 GPT 6.1 Sol agents with the instruction: "win the game." GPTs won our series 6–3, usually by breaking Claude's bed in the final minutes, while Claude played defensively and tried to win on kills.

Bed Wars is a popular game format where teams fight to destroy each other’s bed while protecting their own. In our instance, teams started on separate islands, with currency spawners between them in no-man’s-land. Agents could build bridges to cross between islands and buy upgrades using currency collected in the center of the map.

A team wins by destroying the opposing side’s bed, then killing their remaining players. As long as a team’s bed is present, players respawn after dying. Once a team’s bed is destroyed, their players no longer respawn, meaning their next death eliminates them from the match. This may seem complicated, but think of the team’s main objective as defending their bed and destroying their opponent’s. That said, if no beds were destroyed in a given match, the team with the most kills won.

In almost every run, the GPT agents were much more aggressive and coordinated in their strategies to destroy the Claude team’s bed. This was an inherently riskier strategy vs. Claude’s more defensive posture that tried to win by kill count.

The two teams had very different communication styles. GPT almost immediately started using truncated forms of speech: “First leg complete x32 z9..24 y100.” Claude signed its name and said "we" (30% of messages, against GPT's 5%). GPT sent 5-30x more messages. Its most-messaged player got 198–368 DMs a game; Claude's got 11–48.

GPT agents came up with much more aggressive and elaborate strategies. They would storm the center platforms and farm currency, then use those upgrades to relentlessly attack the other team using constructed bridges, ranged weapons, and Ender Pearls for teleportation. The agents also wrote scripts that chained actions together, like Felix’s one-line command that ate a golden apple, equipped an ender pearl, aimed and threw it.

Claude worked out that they’d win on kills if both beds stood, and stopped attacking. The downside was that if a GPT agent got through and broke the bed, the game was effectively lost for the Claudes. In GPT's three wins in the last two series, it broke Claude's bed with about three minutes left. Claude was ahead on kills 63–16, 57–19, and 59–24.

An interesting moment arrived after the GPT team broke their opponent’s bed. Instead of launching into a Hail Mary offensive, their private reasoning showed a re-entrenchment as they shifted to an even more defensive posture.
